en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 24.1 (SN 24.1, PTS SN iii 202) 1. The Chapter on Stream-Entry (Sotāpattivagga) The Discourse on the Wind (Vātasutta) At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is non-self. What is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. "Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is non-self. What is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. "When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, he here discards belief in a self, discards belief in what pertains to a self; he becomes one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit, whose influxes are destroyed, and who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination."
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, by adhering to what, does such a view as this arise:”
“Do the winds not blow? Do the rivers not flow? Do pregnant women not give birth? Do the moon and sun not rise and set, remaining fixed like pillars?
“Venerable sir, our teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, and the Blessed One as their refuge.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of these words. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”
“Therefore, monks, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, when there is form, by clinging to form, by adhering to form, such a view arises:
‘The winds do not blow, rivers do not flow, pregnant women do not give birth, and the moon and sun do not rise or set, but stand fixed like pillars.
When there is feeling … [and so on] …”
When there is perception … when there are volitional formations … when there is consciousness,
by depending on consciousness, by adhering to consciousness, such a view arises:
‘The winds do not blow, rivers do not flow, pregnant women do not give birth, and the moon and sun do not rise or set,
but remain fixed like pillars. What do you think, monks,
is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, Bhante.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, Bhante.”
“But regarding that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—could the view arise, independent of grasping at it, that:
‘Winds do not blow, rivers do not flow, pregnant women do not give birth, and the moon and sun do not rise or set, but stand fixed like a pillar’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Is feeling permanent or impermanent?
… “Is perception … are formations …”
“Is consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But regarding that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, could the view arise without clinging to it thus:
‘Winds do not blow, rivers do not flow, pregnant women do not give birth, and the moon and sun neither rise nor set, but stand firm like pillars’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Is even that which is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and ranged over by the mind permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, venerable sir.”— “But what is impermanent,
suffering, and subject to change— could the view ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’ arise with regard to that without grasping?”
“Do the winds not blow, do the rivers not flow, do pregnant women not give birth, and do the sun and moon not rise and set, but remain fixed like pillars?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple has abandoned doubt regarding these points, and [doubt] regarding suffering as well...”
Doubt has been abandoned; doubt regarding the origin of suffering has been abandoned by him; doubt regarding the cessation of suffering has been abandoned by him;
doubt regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering has been abandoned by him.
This, monks, is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his final goal.”

When volitional formations exist… when consciousness exists,
by depending on consciousness and adhering to consciousness, this view arises:
“This is mine, this I am, this is my self.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 24.3 (SN 24.3, PTS SN iii 204) 1. Sotāpattivagga Soattāsutta (The Discourse on "He Has a Self") At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, do you hold the view: 'The world and the self are eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion'? "No, venerable sir. "Do you hold the view: 'The world and the self are finite... infinite... both finite and infinite... neither finite nor infinite; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion'? "No, venerable sir. "Do you hold the view: 'The Tathāgata exists after death... does not exist after death... both exists and does not exist after death... neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion'? "No, venerable sir. "Bhikkhus, since you do not hold these views, what view do you hold? "Venerable sir, we are disciples who have gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness. "But, bhikkhus, when you were householders, what view did you hold? "Venerable sir, as householders we held various views. "But, bhikkhus, what was the root of those various views? "Desire and lust, venerable sir. "Since desire and lust for these things has been abandoned and cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising, by what means could those views arise again? When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: 'Since desire and lust for these things has been abandoned and cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising, by what means could those views arise again? "It is precisely because of this, Ānanda, that it is called the 'unshaken' (akuppa). For, Ānanda, when one is shaken by identity-view, one is shaken by the view of the existence of a self, by the view of the non-existence of a self, by the view of the finitude of the world, by the view of the infinity of the world, by the view of the Tathāgata’s existence after death, by the view of the Tathāgata’s non-existence after death, by the view of the Tathāgata’s both existence and non-existence after death, and by the view of the Tathāgata’s neither existence nor non-existence after death. But when identity-view is abandoned, the view of the existence of a self is abandoned, the view of the non-existence of a self is abandoned, the view of the finitude of the world is abandoned, the view of the infinity of the world is abandoned, the view of the Tathāgata’s existence after death is abandoned, the view of the Tathāgata’s non-existence after death is abandoned, the view of the Tathāgata’s both existence and non-existence after death is abandoned, and the view of the Tathāgata’s neither existence nor non-existence after death is abandoned. Therefore, Ānanda, it is called the 'unshaken. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: 'Since desire and lust for these things has been abandoned and cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising, by what means could those views arise again? It is precisely because of this, venerable sir, that it is called the 'unshaken. For, venerable sir, when one is shaken by identity-view, one is shaken by the view of the existence of a self... [as above] ...the view of the Tathāgata’s neither existence nor non-existence after death. But when identity-view is abandoned, the view of the existence of a self is abandoned... [as above] ...the view of the Tathāgata’s neither existence nor non-existence after death is abandoned. Therefore, venerable sir, it is called the 'unshaken. "So it is, Ānanda, so it is! It is precisely because of this, Ānanda, that it is called the 'unshaken. For, Ānanda, when one is shaken by identity-view, one is shaken by the view of the existence of a self... [as above] ...the view of the Tathāgata’s neither existence nor non-existence after death. But when identity-view is abandoned, the view of the existence of a self is abandoned... [as above] ...the view of the Tathāgata’s neither existence nor non-existence after death is abandoned. Therefore, Ānanda, it is called the 'unshaken. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda rejoiced in the Blessed One's words. (This concludes the third discourse in the Chapter on Stream-Entry.)

beings of spontaneous birth; there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have fared rightly and practiced rightly, who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make them known.
This person consists of the four great elements; when he dies, earth returns to the body of earth and departs from it.
The water element enters into and goes toward the body of water; the fire element enters into and goes toward the body of fire; the air element enters into and goes toward the body of air.

their footprints are visible only as far as the cremation ground;
the bones turn the color of pigeon droppings.

this giving is merely a conventional designation.

The Karoto Sutta.
Setting: Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, by adhering to what, does such a view arise as this: [that the world is eternal]?"
‘For one who acts or causes to act, who cuts or causes to cut, who cooks or causes to cook, who grieves or causes to grieve, who exerts oneself or causes to exert,
who trembles or causes to tremble; for one who destroys living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into dwellings, plunders by force, commits burglary,
ambushes highways, commits adultery, or speaks falsehood— ’
"No evil is done by him who does not act.
Even if one were to take this earth with the edge of a razor and make it a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, there would be no evil on that account, nor any arrival of evil.

Even if one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges, killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, cooking and causing to cook, there would be no evil on that account, nor any arrival of evil."

“Even if one were to go to the further bank of the Ganges, giving, causing others to give, sacrificing, and causing others to sacrifice, there would be no merit on that account, nor any arrival of merit.
Through giving, self-control, restraint, and speaking the truth, there is no merit, nor any arrival of merit.
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One... [and so forth].

‘There is no doing, no causing to do...
there is no merit, no outcome of merit.’”
When feeling exists …pe… when perception exists … when volitional formations exist …

"There is no doing, there is no causing to do...

[as before] ...would such a view as this arise without clinging to that? “No, venerable sir. “In this way, venerable sir, it should be understood: ‘This is suffering’; in this way, ‘this is the origin of suffering’; in this way, ‘this is the cessation of suffering’; in this way, ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “If, venerable sir, one does not cling to form as ‘my self,’ nor to feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness as ‘my self,’ would such a view as this arise: ‘There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings’; or ‘There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings’; or ‘Beings are defiled without cause or condition’; or ‘Beings are purified without cause or condition’? The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, by adhering to what, does such a view arise as this:

they do not move, they do not change, they do not obstruct one another, and they are incapable of bringing about each other’s pleasure, pain, or both pleasure and pain’?”
Which seven?
The earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, pleasure, pain, and the soul as the seventh.
These seven bodies are unmade, not fashioned by artifice, uncreated, not produced by a creator, barren, fixed like a peak, and standing firm like a pillar.
They do not move, they do not change, and they do not obstruct one another; they are not capable of bringing pleasure, pain, or both pleasure and pain to one another.
Even when one cuts off someone’s head with a sharp sword, that person does not deprive anyone of life;
rather, the sword merely passes through the opening between the seven bodies.
Now, there are these fourteen hundred thousand principal wombs,
sixty-six hundred, five hundred actions, five actions, three actions, action and half-action, sixty-two paths,
sixty-two intermediate eons, six classes of birth, eight stages of manhood, and four hundred and ninety-nine modes of livelihood.
Forty-nine hundred wanderers, forty-nine hundred abodes of nāgas, twenty hundred faculties, thirty hundred hells,
thirty-six elements of dust, seven types of womb for those with perception, seven types of womb for those without perception, seven types of womb for the Nigaṇṭhas,

There are hundreds of births in hell, seven dreams, seven hundred dreams, and eighty-four thousand great aeons, which fools and the wise alike must run through and wander about before they will make an end of suffering.
In this regard, there is no [thought]: "By means of this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall ripen unripened karma."

“‘I shall bring to an end each instance of matured karma as it arises’—this is not possible. Pleasure and pain are measured out like a grain-measure; saṃsāra is limited, with no decrease or increase, no waxing or waning.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 24.10 (SN 24.10, PTS SN iii 214) 1. The Chapter on Stream-Entry The Discourse on the View of Eternity At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. This, bhikkhus, is called the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). “Or, bhikkhus, regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging, one might hold the view: ‘It is not eternal. This, bhikkhus, is called the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). “Any ascetic or brahmin who holds the view of eternalism, bhikkhus, does so in dependence upon these same five aggregates subject to clinging; none other than these five aggregates subject to clinging. Any ascetic or brahmin who holds the view of annihilationism, bhikkhus, does so in dependence upon these same five aggregates subject to clinging; none other than these five aggregates subject to clinging. “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to say: ‘I will make a fire using only this kind of wood and this kind of grass, and I will not make a fire using any other kind of wood or any other kind of grass. That man would be incapable of doing so. Why is that? Because it is impossible for him to do so. So too, bhikkhus, any ascetic or brahmin who holds the view of eternalism or the view of annihilationism does so in dependence upon these same five aggregates subject to clinging; none other than these five aggregates subject to clinging. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and departed. Then, soon after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend! those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed, he did so intending to teach the Dhamma concerning the five aggregates subject to clinging. “What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging... [as above] ...none other than these five aggregates subject to clinging. “Friends, if anyone should say: ‘Apart from these five aggregates subject to clinging, I will declare another self possessed of form, permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and the same as I,’ that would be an empty, hollow, and false claim. Why is that? Because, friends, apart from these five aggregates subject to clinging, no other self is found that is permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and the same as I. “Friends, if anyone should say: ‘Apart from these five aggregates subject to clinging, I will declare another self without form, permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and the same as I,’ that would be an empty, hollow, and false claim. Because, friends, apart from these five aggregates subject to clinging, no other self is found that is without form, permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and the same as I. “Friends, if anyone should say: ‘Apart from these five aggregates subject to clinging, I will declare another self both with form and without form, permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and the same as I,’ that would be an empty, hollow, and false claim. Why is that? Because, friends, apart from these five aggregates subject to clinging, no other self is found that is both with form and without form, permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and the same as I. “Friends, if anyone should say: ‘Apart from these five aggregates subject to clinging, I will declare another self neither with form nor without form, permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and the same as I,’ that would be an empty, hollow, and false claim. Why is that? Because, friends, apart from these five aggregates subject to clinging, no other self is found that is neither with form nor without form, permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and the same as I.

“Friends, if anyone should say: ‘Apart from these five aggregates subject to clinging, I will declare another self percipient, permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and the same as I,’ that would be an empty, hollow, and false claim. Why is that? Because, friends, apart from these five aggregates subject to clinging, no other self is found that is percipient, permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and the same as I. “Friends, if anyone should say: ‘Apart from these five aggregates subject to clinging, I will declare another self non-percipient, permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and the same as I,’ that would be an empty, hollow, and false claim. Why is that? Why is that? Sotāpattivagga Antavāsutta (The Discourse on the Finite) “Bhikkhus, those ascetics and brahmins who speculate about the finite and the infinite, and who hold views concerning the finite and the infinite—all these venerable ones, whatever they may say, all that is included within these four positions, or it falls short of them, or it exceeds them. What four? (1) ‘The self and the world are finite after death’—this is the first position. (2) ‘The self and the world are infinite after death’—this is the second position. (3) ‘The self and the world are both finite and infinite after death’—this is the third position. (4) ‘The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite after death’—this is the fourth position. Those ascetics and brahmins who speculate about the finite and the infinite, and who hold views concerning the finite and the infinite—all these venerable ones, whatever they may say, all that is included within these four positions, or it falls short of them, or it exceeds them. Now, bhikkhus, if anyone should say thus: ‘I will refute the speculative view of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views concerning the finite and the infinite,’ even if he were to speak for an aeon, he would not be able to refute them, and moreover, he would become fatigued. Why is that? Because this Dhamma is profound, hard to see, hard to comprehend, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and comprehensible only to the wise. It is difficult for those who follow other doctrines to understand it. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall understand as it really is the meaning and the Dhamma of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views concerning the finite and the infinite. Thus, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 24.12 (SN 24.12, PTS SN iii 215) 1. Sotāpattivagga Anantavāsutta (The Discourse on Infinity) At Sāvatthī. “Venerable sir, it was said by the Blessed One: ‘The world is infinite; this is the truth, and anything else is false. How far, venerable sir, does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhus, if one were to say: ‘The world is finite,’ that would be a wrong view. If one were to say: ‘The world is infinite,’ that too would be a wrong view. If one were to say: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ that too would be a wrong view. If one were to say: ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ that too would be a wrong view. If one were to say: ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ that too would be a wrong view. If one were to say: ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ that too would be a wrong view. “But, venerable sir, if all these are wrong views, what then is the right view? “Bhikkhus, when one sees with correct wisdom as it really is: ‘This is suffering’—this is right view. When one sees with correct wisdom as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’—this is right view. When one sees with correct wisdom as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—this is right view. When one sees with correct wisdom as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—this is right view. “Venerable sir, if one sees with correct wisdom as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ how far does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhu, when one sees with correct wisdom as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ one is then a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, with a fixed destiny. “Venerable sir, if one is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, with a fixed destiny, how far does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhu, when one is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, with a fixed destiny, one has transcended birth in the hells, the animal realm, and the sphere of afflicted spirits; one has transcended states of deprivation, the evil destination, and the lower world. This is the extent of the teaching. “Venerable sir, if one has transcended birth in the hells, the animal realm, and the sphere of afflicted spirits; if one has transcended states of deprivation, the evil destination, and the lower world, how far does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhu, when one has transcended birth in the hells, the animal realm, and the sphere of afflicted spirits; when one has transcended states of deprivation, the evil destination, and the lower world—one is then a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, with a fixed destiny. This is the extent of the teaching. “Venerable sir, if one is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, with a fixed destiny, and has transcended birth in the hells, the animal realm, and the sphere of afflicted spirits; if one has transcended states of deprivation, the evil destination, and the lower world—how far does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhu, when one is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, with a fixed destiny, and has transcended birth in the hells, the animal realm, and the sphere of afflicted spirits; when one has transcended states of deprivation, the evil destination, and the lower world—one is then incapable of doing any deed by which one might be reborn in hell, the animal realm, or the sphere of afflicted spirits. This is the extent of the teaching. “Venerable sir, if one is incapable of doing any deed by which one might be reborn in hell, the animal realm, or the sphere of afflicted spirits, how far does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhu, when one is incapable of doing any deed by which one might be reborn in hell, the animal realm, or the sphere of afflicted spirits—one is then incapable of passing away without having realized the fruit of stream-entry. This is the extent of the teaching. “Venerable sir, if one is incapable of passing away without having realized the fruit of stream-entry, how far does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhu, when one is incapable of passing away without having realized the fruit of stream-entry—one is then incapable of being reborn in a family of outcasts or scavengers, or in a family of hunters, fishermen, or chariot-makers; one is incapable of being reborn in a family lacking the seven treasures. This is the extent of the teaching. “Venerable sir, if one is incapable of being reborn in a family of outcasts or scavengers, or in a family of hunters, fishermen, or chariot-makers;

if one is incapable of being reborn in a family lacking the seven treasures, how far does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhu, when one is incapable of being reborn in a family of outcasts or scavengers, or in a family of hunters, fishermen, or chariot-makers; when one is incapable of being reborn in a family lacking the seven treasures—one is then incapable of being reborn in a family other than those of khattiyas, brahmins, or householders. This is the extent of the teaching. “Venerable sir, if one is incapable of being reborn in a family other than those of khattiyas, brahmins, or householders, how far does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhu, when one is incapable of being reborn in a family other than those of khattiyas, brahmins, or householders—one is then incapable of being reborn in a family that is not wealthy, prosperous, or affluent. This is the extent of the teaching. “Venerable sir, if one is incapable of being reborn in a family that is not wealthy, prosperous, or affluent, how far does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhu, when one is incapable of being reborn in a family that is not wealthy, prosperous, or affluent—one is then incapable of being reborn in a family that lacks the seven treasures. This is the extent of the teaching. “Venerable sir, if one is incapable of being reborn in a family that lacks the seven treasures, how far does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhu, when one is incapable of being reborn in a family that lacks the seven treasures—one is then incapable of being reborn in a family other than those of khattiyas, brahmins, or householders. This is the extent of the teaching. “Venerable sir, if one is incapable of being reborn in a family other than those of khattiyas, brahmins, or householders; if one is incapable of being reborn in a family that is not wealthy, prosperous, or affluent; if one is incapable of being reborn in a family that lacks the seven treasures—how far does this teaching extend? “Bhikkhu, when one is incapable of being reborn in a family other than those of khattiyas, brahmins, or householders; when one is incapable of being reborn in a family that is not wealthy, prosperous, or affluent; when one is incapable of being reborn in a family that lacks the seven treasures—one is then incapable of being reborn in a family that is not well-born, of noble lineage, or of ancient descent. Sotāpattivagga Nahotitathāgatosutta (The Discourse on Whether a Tathāgata Exists) At Sāvatthī. “Venerable sir, does a Tathāgata exist after death? “Vakkali, I do not say that ‘a Tathāgata exists after death. “But, venerable sir, does a Tathāgata not exist after death? “Vakkali, I do not say that ‘a Tathāgata does not exist after death. “Then, venerable sir, does a Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death? “Vakkali, I do not say that ‘a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death. “But, venerable sir, does a Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death? “Vakkali, I do not say that ‘a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. “Why is it, venerable sir, that the Blessed One does not say: ‘a Tathāgata exists after death’; or ‘a Tathāgata does not exist after death’; or ‘a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’; or ‘a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’? “Because, Vakkali, these do not pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life, they are not connected with the fundamentals of the holy life, and they do not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna. This, Vakkali, pertains to the fundamentals of the holy life, is connected with the fundamentals of the holy life, and leads to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
